headings.title: Memory Editor reads, revisions and persistence

html:
Memory Editor reads, revisions and persistence

Memory Editor is a human editing client for the existing Memory store. Its browser form, the active stored revision and the latest disk checkpoint are three separate states. The client preserves a draft when a write is rejected and uses the loaded record revision to prevent a save or delete from overwriting a newer edit.

memory_editor.js owns inventory paging, selection, form state, explicit mutations and persistence feedback. MemoryRoutes validates requests, binds the existing Memory editor service and returns checkpoint targets after successful mutations. The API and maintenance contract defines payloads and storage behavior; Memory storage owns recall, identity and transaction semantics. User controls are described in Memory Editor.

Data ownership

flowchart TD User[Human editor] --> Draft[Local form and dirty baseline] Draft --> Intent[Explicit create, update or delete intent] Revision[Loaded record revision] --> Intent Intent --> Route[Authenticated Memory API] Route -->|Create or update| Service[MemoryEditor validation and projection] Route -->|Delete with expected revision| Store Service --> Store[Authoritative Memory store] Store --> Active[Published active revision] Active --> Detail[Committed detail and persistence metadata] Detail --> Draft Store --> Inventory[Inventory snapshot and summary pages] Inventory --> Browser[Search, filters and selected record] Browser --> Draft Active --> Checkpoint[Existing checkpoint owner] Checkpoint --> Disk[Disk recovery generation] Checkpoint --> Diagnostics[Persistence diagnostics] Diagnostics --> Banner[Latest mutation's disk-save status] Detail --> Banner

The browser transports content as text with an explicit text or json format. It does not parse JSON content before sending it, so integers beyond JavaScript number precision reach the server intact. Only the source-reference field is parsed locally, as an array of strings. Tags, recall summary and project selection remain separate metadata. Saving or viewing this editor does not call a model, dispatch Memory tools, grant inspection credit or create an execution receipt.

Initialization loads inventory and available Gateway choices independently, then opens an optional ?key= selection. Failure to load Gateway choices is reported; it does not erase an existing project binding. Gateway choices describe saved identities. These reads and saves do not probe a Gateway or establish that a remote folder exists.

Inventory, selection and refresh

sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant B as Inventory browser participant A as Memory API participant F as Selected form U->>B: Search, filter, refresh or load more B->>B: Capture query and advance list generation B->>A: GET summaries with limit 50 and current offset A-->>B: Entries, counts, tags and inventory revision alt Response belongs to an obsolete generation B->>B: Ignore response else Appended page has a different inventory revision B->>A: Restart from offset zero A-->>B: Fresh first page else Current page belongs to expected inventory B->>B: Replace or append literal summary rows end U->>B: Select a different memory or explicitly reload B->>F: Check pending work and confirm draft discard if needed opt Selection allowed B->>A: GET encoded key alt Detail available A-->>F: Content text, metadata and revision F->>F: Adopt detail and reset dirty baseline else Read rejected A-->>F: Error F->>F: Preserve prior form and show feedback end end

Pages contain 50 summaries. Search waits 180 ms after input before issuing the next read, but invalidates older list responses immediately. Tag and scope changes issue reads directly. Each request captures its own generation; only the current one can replace list state or release its busy indicator. Appending a page with a different inventory revision restarts pagination instead of silently skipping or duplicating rows after a concurrent edit. The server's list revision does not lock the inventory for subsequent requests.

Selecting the already-open key returns to the editor view without reloading its form. A different key or explicit Reload checks for an active save/detail read and asks before discarding a dirty draft. Accepted detail resets the form baseline, loaded revision, project-rebinding toggle and selected URL. Existing keys remain read-only. Text is inserted literally into summary rows; detail content remains editable text rather than executable markup.

Refresh reloads summaries, then checks the captured selected record again if it is still selected. A changed revision offers Reload while keeping the local draft. It does not automatically paint the competing edit over the form. Reload requires the same discard confirmation. Navigation links use that confirmation, and the browser unload handler requests its standard warning for dirty or saving state. Returning from the narrow editor pane to the inventory preserves the form.

Explicit write and conflict sequence

sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant F as Local form participant A as Memory API participant M as Memory service and store participant P as Checkpoint owner U->>F: Save or confirm Delete F->>F: Check pending work and validate local fields F->>A: POST create, PUT edit or DELETE with revision A->>A: Validate request and supplied Gateway identity alt Request validation fails A-->>F: HTTP validation error F-->>U: Preserve draft and show feedback else Request valid A->>M: Create or apply expected-revision mutation alt Store validation, absence or revision conflict M-->>A: Rejection A-->>F: HTTP error F-->>U: Keep draft and show Reload when applicable else Mutation accepted M-->>A: Committed result opt Running RAM checkpointer A->>P: Request a checkpoint target P-->>A: Target generation epoch and revision end A-->>F: Mutation result and persistence metadata F->>F: Adopt save or clear deleted selection F->>A: Refresh summary inventory F-->>U: Active change and separate persistence feedback end end

The browser validates key syntax, requires tags for new records, requires a recall summary for new/project/previously described records, and checks that source references are strings. It sends content without interpreting JSON. Server validation still owns strict JSON, size limits, normalized key uniqueness, descriptor rules, Gateway existence and absolute project roots.

Existing writes include the loaded expected_revision; new creation uses a create-only POST. Delete requires confirmation and the loaded revision, including when an unsaved local draft would also be discarded. A 404/409 response exposes Reload when a relevant key is available. Other validation or transport errors also keep the form. An uncertain transport outcome is not proof that no mutation occurred; refresh/reload lets the user inspect current saved truth before deciding what to do.

The project section preserves an existing binding by omitting replacement inputs from the request unless the user explicitly chooses Change project binding. New or newly project-scoped records require a chosen Gateway and nonempty folder in the browser; the server checks the absolute-root contract. A legacy opaque binding can therefore survive ordinary content edits even when its original folder cannot be displayed.

Save is enabled only for a dirty idle form. During save/delete or a detail read, competing editor controls are disabled. Acknowledged save adopts the returned committed detail, including semantic no-op responses; acknowledged delete clears selection. Inventory refresh failure can leave the list stale after a successful mutation; the stored result and list observation remain separate. Explicit controls and Ctrl/Cmd+S use the same save path.

Active changes and disk confirmation

sequenceDiagram participant F as Mutation response handler participant O as Persistence observer participant A as Persistence status endpoint participant P as Checkpoint diagnostics F->>O: Start latest mutation observation alt Synchronous disk save reported O->>O: Display saved to disk else No checkpoint target available O->>O: Display active change with unavailable disk status else Checkpoint target present loop Until target matches, superseded, read fails or document closes O->>A: GET persistence status A->>P: Read diagnostics from RAM P-->>O: Last good epoch, checkpoint revision and error state alt Epoch matches and revision reaches target O->>O: Confirm saved to disk and stop else Checkpoint has not reached target O->>O: Display pending or needs-attention status O->>O: Wait 1.5 seconds before next read end end end Note over O,A: A transport error stops this chain with unavailable status Note over F,O: A newer successful mutation supersedes older checks

The persistence status route reads checkpoint diagnostics from RAM. A pending target is confirmed only when last_good_generation_epoch equals its target_epoch and last_checkpoint_revision reaches its target_revision. Comparing only revision numbers across different recovery generations would not establish the requested write's durability.

Store publication and checkpoint-target response construction are separate stages. An error in a later stage does not establish that the earlier store mutation rolled back; inspect the current record before deciding whether to retry.

The observer requests status immediately, then repeats after 1.5 seconds while the target remains pending. A reported checkpointer error changes the message to “needs attention” while observation continues. A transport failure reports unavailable status and stops that chain. A newer successful mutation advances the local observer generation, preventing an older check from replacing its feedback. There is no fixed retry count or timeout in this component.

Selecting another memory does not reset the persistence banner: it describes the latest observed mutation. The banner is outside the selected-record panel, so delete confirmation remains visible after that panel closes. Active publication does not by itself establish disk durability; requesting a checkpoint and observing its completion are separate steps. Standalone synchronous storage can report disk confirmation directly; unavailable/stopped RAM checkpointing can leave an accepted mutation with no target and no disk confirmation.

Browser fixtures exercise conflicts, failed saves, preserved drafts, project rebinding, duplicate creation, changed-inventory pagination and visible delete persistence with local isolated state. Theme-specific acceptance is outside this review. The service/API fixtures provide the existing storage and payload contract evidence.
